newsitem.title: USA: S. Carolina Klan museum claims to teach history.
newsitem.headline: S. Carolina Klan museum claims to teach history.

text.p: John Howard has opened his Ku Klux Klan Museum just off the town square in this small northwestern South Carolina city, just as he said he would.
For many here the museum serves as a constant reminder of the racial strife that has split this community for so long.
"It is a big atrocity. It has the potential of initiating a race war," said Rev. David Kennedy, pastor of New Beginning Church.

It stirs the same feelings among African Americans as the rope that hung for 75 years from a railroad trestle. Situated at the entrance to town from the black community, it invoked the message, "Stay in your place."
The rope killed Kennedy's great-great uncle Richard Puckett, who was wrongly accused of raping a white woman.

Last March Howard's first commercial venture, the Redneck Shop, whipped up a firestorm of criticism from city fathers and civil rights activist the Rev. Jesse Jackson, who visited here to show his opposition.
Bricks were thrown through the windows and a driver rammed his car into the front of the building. Howard's partner left him and cancelled the shop's business license, which was in his name.
Howard continued to operate anyway. Last week, realising there were no grounds to deny it, the City Council reluctantly issued a business license to Howard.

The museum offers the milder side of the 129-year-old KKK, from its founding by Confederate Gen. Nathan Bedford Forest in the aftermath of the Civil War to its heyday in the 1960s, when white-robed and hooded members threatened blacks and white liberals by staging torchlit parades and setting fire to crosses on their lawns. It has drawn diehard fans and the just-plain-curious.

Howard, 50, said the museum will help people remember the savageness of the Klan and help prevent such brutality from happening again. A former member of the Keystone Knights of the KKK, he said he wants to teach the Klan history.
"It's our heritage that should not be forgotten," Howard said. "Do you want to destroy all the crematories? If you do then there will be more."

Business has been slow but steady, according to Howard, who sells T-shirts bearing Confederate symbols or racist sayings, along with ceramic lamps in the form of a Klansman and knives with KKK embossed on the blade.

Pictures make up most of the exhibit, with particular emphasis on Klansmen Howard has known. There are photos of women Klan members and children in white robes, a hospital in Atlanta and an orphanage run by the Klan. One poster says, "Don't be half a man. Join the Klan."
Hanging from the ceiling in the central room are robes, a half dozen or more, some fashioned of crude cotton, others ornate, made of a silky material and decorated with decals.

Howard also has a number of trinkets, from KKK rings to buttons, a cross and some knives. Books and pamphlets tell the Klan story, including one that outlines how to have a Klan funeral. In a display case rests a pad of "fiery summons," the forms used to force members to attend meetings and lynchings.

The raw brutality of the Klan is not apparent in Howard's museum. He said he owns photographs of lynchings and other hate crimes but will not display them because he wants children to be able to visit.

One small black-and-white photograph shows a young African American being branded by two robed men. Also displayed are three small signs from the days of segregation. They say "Public pool Whites Only," "Colored Must Sit in Balcony" and "No Dogs Negroes Mexicans."
"I warn everybody about messing with Klans," said Howard. "It's not for me to judge but it is for me to explain."
Kennedy does not believe Howard seeks only to educate.

"The KKK has always been deceptive," he said, promising more rallies against Howard, his shop and his museum. "We will always know we can't trust the KKK. These things haunt the community. They haunt our nation."
